extracted.intended_audience: travellers, students of art and architecture, and scholars of Venetian/Gothic sculpture
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive and evaluative analysis of the carved capitals and sculpture of the Ducal Palace in Venice, giving criteria for reading, dating, and judging workmanship, iconography, and expressive qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciation of dignity in features
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is more remarkable in all early sculpture, than its appreciation of the signs of dignity of character in the features, and the way in which it can exalt the principal figure in any subject by a few touches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether facial features and small emphatic details convey dignity and elevate the principal figure; look for economy of means (a few touches) that produce strong character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legibility and reading of inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Inscriptions on capitals (often Latin or dialect) are essential for interpretation; where legible, give the letters as they stand and then propose readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record inscriptions exactly (including doubtful letters in brackets), note contractions/marks, and use them for identification, iconography, and dating; missing or defaced inscriptions limit interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iconographic accuracy and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects (e.g. planets in their zodiacal 'houses') should be placed and arranged to convey intended meanings such as season or astrological house; positions may indicate time of year when the cornerstone was laid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether figures/furnishings are positioned meaningfully (e.g., the sun in Leo, moon in Cancer) and whether the arrangement supports the intended symbolic reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to epigraphic marks and punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Small marks (comma-like contraction marks, zigzag marks, dot/period signs) appear on the stones and affect reading of inscriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note and interpret epigraphic signs when transcribing inscriptions; these can change word divisions, contractions, and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive use of drapery
rubrics_metrics.description: Drapery treatment should serve expressive intent: 'severe but full folds, showing little of the forms beneath them' for some figures, or rippling folds to suggest special effects (e.g., moonlight on waves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the fold treatment matches the subject's character or the sculptor's idea (e.g., moon's rippling drapery to suggest light), avoiding generic or irrelevant handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculptural technique to harness light (undercutting/relief depth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Undercutting and relief depth are used to make parts 'glitter in the light' or to create striking highlights (e.g., fish or leaves contrasted with deep gloom below).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine carving depth and undercutting to see how light/dark contrast enhances forms; assess if these techniques are used intentionally for visual effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of mass and surface detail
rubrics_metrics.description: A powerful capital combines 'broad massiveness' of general form with fine 'minute chasing' or delicate surface detail (plumage of birds, clustered bees), the contrast enhancing ornamental value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the relationship between strong overall composition and the finesse of surface carving; good work balances monumentality with detailed finish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vitality and naturalism versus hardness
rubrics_metrics.description: Superior work shows 'grace, life, and variety' in figures and foliage; earlier earliness may be marked by 'hardness and coldness' in large heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether figures/animals exhibit naturalistic life and variety or whether they are stiff/harsh; consider whether perceived hardness is a period trait or a defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compositional skill and arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups and arrangements (of figures, foliage, fruit, etc.) should be well composed in mass and in relation to the capital's function as a distant, architectural element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge overall grouping, balance, and the way forms read at a distance; strong composition is essential for capitals intended for 'hard service and distant effect.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality versus copying (invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Renaissance work is often criticized for a 'total want of invention' when merely copying earlier models; originality and invention are valued virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish genuine invention and variation from mere plagiarism or slavish copying; originality in motif, grouping, or treatment is a positive quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and significance of color/inlay
rubrics_metrics.description: Inlaying of small colored stones (serpentine, red marble, etc.) in capitals expresses the architect's feeling for color and inlay as essential to the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note any inlaid colored stones and evaluate their ornamental and symbolic roles; color can be an intentional and meaningful component of the design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate depiction of occupations and attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures representing trades or professions should carry appropriate tools/implements and convey the occupation convincingly (e.g., lapicida with hammer, carpentarius planing a beam).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess iconographic accuracy of attributes and actions; clear, believable depiction aids identification and the capital's communicative function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic features as dating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific formal traits (capital forms, drapery style, window order, tool forms, dialect of inscriptions) can determine a date or century of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distinctive stylistic markers and inscriptions to date elements (e.g., fifth order windows typical of early fourteenth century) and to identify restorations or later insertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and appropriateness of inscriptions (not redundant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inscribed names/labels can aid interpretation, but unnecessary or overly explicit labels (e.g., naming obvious fruits) may be superfluous and disrespectful of the viewer's intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer inscriptions that add meaningful information; note when labeling is redundant or when inscriptions reveal the sculptor's intent or audience assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic coherence and devotional/intellectual intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitals often express themes (ages of man, arts, justice, marriage history) and may reveal devotional spirit or civic principles; alternation of saints and workmen expresses devotion in workmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the series of subjects coheres thematically and whether symbolic choices (saints, allegories) align with intended moral, civic, or devotional messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philological and linguistic evidence in inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Orthography and letter forms (e.g., 'o for e', u for o) in inscriptions preserve pronunciation and provide historical linguistic evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine spellings and dialect usage as part of analysis; these features can illuminate contemporary pronunciation, language use, and dating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to small, telling details (ornamental motifs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Minute devices—trefoiled studs, ring-shaped ears on lions, bees on honeycombs, carved cherry stalks—are significant in assessing craftsmanship and period character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect small patented motifs and technical details; they can indicate regional style, chronological phase, and the sculptor's skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for site and viewing conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Work intended for the palace must be 'meant for hard service and distant effect'—materials, scale, and compositional clarity should suit exposure and viewing distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge materials, scale, and boldness of forms relative to site (sea wind exposure, viewing from piazza); durability and legibility at distance are essential.
